summary: Weekly POC check-in for Orbit Analytics pilot. Reviewed latest TTFT and streaming traces, discussed sequence length distribution impacts, and kernel selection tradeoffs. Agreed to run a focused microburst workload and exchange trimmed perf artifacts. Action items assigned to SE and Orbit ML lead.
topics: TTFT, streaming handshake, sequence-length distribution, kernel fastpath vs hedging, KV/prefix caching, Dedicated burst pricing
transcript:
00:00 Jordan Miller: All right, thanks everyone for joining. quick roll call?
00:06 Maya Rodriguez: Maya here.
00:08 Ethan Park: Ethan on.
00:09 Sofia Li: Sofia.
00:11 Tom Weber: Tom.
00:13 Priya Patel: Priya from Redwood. Luis is on but muted.
00:17 Luis Chen: (unmuted) hey all.
00:20 Jordan Miller: Great. Agenda: go over the Friday perf dump, TTFT numbers that looked a bit spiky, discuss streaming handshakes and then agree next steps.
00:31 Maya Rodriguez: Sounds good. We pushed the 2.7 build last night, so the traces you have should include the new quantized variant.
00:38 Priya Patel: Got it. Quick note — some of our labels in the dump might have model name mangled, the pipeline label sometimes shows as "Redwood-quant" which is the 8-bit qproc; not to be confused with your local model name.
00:48 Ethan Park: Yeah we saw that. We also noticed TTFT median went down but the 95th jumped during microbursts at around 14:20 in the trace.
00:58 Priya Patel: Right, that's the microburst behavior we flagged. The big question: is the 95th due to kernel fallback/heap thrash or due to rehydrating KV cache for longer sequences?
01:12 Sofia Li: Our seqlen dist is bimodal — 60% at 32 tokens, 30% at 320 tokens and 10% at 1024. So when a long one hits and something else is streaming we see a tail.
01:25 Luis Chen: That distribution explains a lot. When long sequences come in they cause both longer KV populate time and also different kernel selection if the runtime hedges to the safer kernel. Hedging can add 20-60ms depending on size.
01:40 Tom Weber: Can you remind us what "hedging" means here? I thought hedging just meant we had two GPUs ready.
01:46 Priya Patel: In our context hedging is runtime choosing a slower but more memory-stable kernel when the fastpath appears risky — e.g., quantization fast kernel that assumes certain stride. If the runtime detects mismatch it falls back mid-request which can add a little spike.
02:02 Jordan Miller: Important: that fallback is automated; we can toggle hedging aggressiveness per route for the pilot.
02:08 Maya Rodriguez: We'd like more deterministic behavior — can we prefer predictability over average latency?
02:13 Priya Patel: Absolutely. Options: 1) force fastpath for a route (lower average, but risk rare errors), 2) force stabilized kernel (slightly higher median but tight tail), 3) enable pre-warm prefix caching for the long sequences so runtime doesn't need to rehydrate KV.
02:30 Ethan Park: We tried pre-warm caching but our upstream client doesn't always send the same prefix because they include a session token; it's noisy.
02:37 Priya Patel: We can add a prefix normalization step in the pipeline to strip session tokens before caching — quick config change. Might help the cache hit rate.
02:45 Sofia Li: That would be helpful. Also, where do we stand on streaming handshake latency? The chunk negotiation seems to add 25-35ms.
02:55 Luis Chen: The handshake overhead has two parts: HTTP/2 frame negotiation and the runtime's initial chunk buffer allocation. We shipped a small tweak last week to reduce buffer allocation time; the traces show 10-12ms improvement on average but bursts remain.
03:13 Jordan Miller: Does the pilot run use continuous batching? That also affects TTFT for the first token depending on how we warm pools.
03:20 Ethan Park: We left continuous batching on default; maybe turning it off for low-concurrency routes would help TTFT.
03:26 Priya Patel: Continuous batching is great for throughput but it can add latency if your traffic is spiky. For TTFT it's often better to pin a tiny pool with warm threads or use the dedicated burst option for those routes.
03:39 Tom Weber: Can you outline the tradeoffs in numbers? Like median vs 95th for each setting?
03:45 Priya Patel: Sure. From last night's CSV: default runtime (continuous batching on) — median TTFT 48ms, 95th 210ms. Forced stable kernel — median 62ms, 95th 120ms. Fastpath forced — median 40ms, 95th 360ms (rare fallbacks amplify). With prefix caching for the 320/1024 group we saw median 53ms, 95th 95ms.
04:10 Maya Rodriguez: Wait that prefix caching stat is much better — what's the catch?
04:14 Luis Chen: The catch is hit rate. If you can normalize prefixes and get hit rate above ~70% for that cohort you see the benefit. If hit rate is low you pay cache overhead without wins.
04:26 Ethan Park: Our current hit rate is around 22% because of the session token variance.
04:30 Priya Patel: Normalization usually brings it to 80-90% for the common cases. We'll provide a normalization config and a small client-side middleware snippet.
04:40 Tom Weber: And the kernel selection — is there a way to signal the runtime from the client? We have heuristics in our proxy that can mark a request as short or long.
04:48 Priya Patel: Yes, you can add a header like x-redwood-pref-kernel: stable|fast|auto. We'll document it. That header will steer the runtime to prefer a kernel, subject to safety checks.
04:58 Jordan Miller: Good. On the microburst runs, Ethan, what was the concurrency pattern?
05:03 Ethan Park: We simulated 80 concurrent short chats with occasional 10 long ones. The long ones are concentrated in 10-second windows — that's where the 95th spikes.
05:12 Priya Patel: That pattern is classic microburst. Two levers: hedging policy and burst capacity. If you enable Dedicated burst option for those routes you get pre-warmed GPUs to absorb spikes; cost goes up a bit but the tail is much tighter.
05:28 Maya Rodriguez: Can you quantify the Dedicated burst cost? We need ballpark for the procurement folks.
05:33 Jordan Miller: We'll send detailed numbers but quick estimate: add ~15-25% incremental cost for the pilot per peak hour depending on GPU type. We'll include exact numbers in the follow-up.
05:42 Sofia Li: We'd prefer to try software mitigations before buying more capacity.
05:45 Luis Chen: Agreed — usually normalization + header steering + enforced stable kernel for the long cohort reduces 95th by ~60-70% without cost changes.
05:56 Tom Weber: How about the streaming chunk size? Can we increase chunk size to reduce handshake overhead?
06:02 Priya Patel: Increasing chunk size reduces total number of frames but increases per-chunk latency; there's a sweet spot. For your workloads we found 8KB chunks were best vs default 4KB, shaved ~12ms on average. We'll include the config diff.
06:18 Ethan Park: Awesome. On the kernel side, what's the difference between fastpath and the quantized fallback we saw? Is the fallback the 4-bit variant?
06:27 Priya Patel: The fallback in this case is the stabilized 8-bit kernel. Fastpath is a specialized kernel optimized for sequence alignment and streaming. The quantized 4-bit path is experimental in this pilot — it can be fastest but is more sensitive to layout.
06:39 Maya Rodriguez: So for safety we should probably route 1024-level sequences to the stable 8-bit until we confirm correctness.
06:45 Priya Patel: That's a safe approach. We can make a per-route rule: if expected seqlen > 512, force stable.
06:52 Ethan Park: How do we set "expected seqlen"? Is that client provided?
06:56 Priya Patel: You can send x-redwood-expected-seqlen header or runtime can estimate from recent traffic and apply heuristics. For this pilot I'd recommend explicit header until you're comfortable.
07:06 Jordan Miller: Let's talk diagnostics: we shared raw perf logs but some fields are dense. Priya, can you create a trimmed view with the fields Orbit cares about?
07:14 Priya Patel: Yes. We'll trim to: request_id, route, kernel_used, ttft_ms, first_chunk_ms, kv_populate_ms, fallback_flag, seqlen, timestamp. We'll also annotate events where hedging/fallback occurred.
07:28 Ethan Park: Perfect. That will help us map the long ones.
07:31 Tom Weber: One more question: SLOs. Right now we have internal target of median <60ms and 95th <150ms. Are those reachable without Dedicated?
07:40 Priya Patel: With the normalization + header steering + stable kernel for long cohort, yes likely. But those are contingent on getting prefix cache hit rate up and avoiding mid-request fallback. If after software changes the 95th still spikes we recommend short Dedicated burst windows during peak.
07:59 Maya Rodriguez: OK. Can you show where in the app flow we add the normalization? Is it client SDK or our edge proxy?
08:05 Priya Patel: We'll give you both options. Quick win is an edge proxy rule that strips or hashes session tokens before caching. SDK change is better long-term. We'll include a small Node/Go snippet.
08:18 Luis Chen: Also FYI—there's a runtime flag we can flip to reduce the hedging sensitivity threshold so it only falls back on very high-risk cases. That reduces rare spikes but slightly increases chance of a silent correctness issue if model layout differs. We don't recommend enabling without model validation tests.
08:34 Ethan Park: Understood. We'll keep hedging conservative but try the normalized cache first.
08:39 Jordan Miller: Cool. Quick recap then next steps before we open up for Qs.
08:43 Jordan Miller: Recap: Redwood to produce trimmed perf CSV and kernel notes; Redwood to provide prefix normalization snippet and header steering doc; Orbit to run 5k seeded pass with --bundle-kernel=fastpath and with and without normalization and share histograms; schedule microburst run next Tuesday; pricing note for Dedicated burst will be sent.
09:05 Tom Weber: Sounds right. Couple quick Qs — is there a log link for the raw traces?
09:10 Priya Patel: Yes we uploaded to the shared S3 link in the pilot folder — I'll paste after the call. Note: some S3 filenames have epoch timestamps and the naming got truncated in the dump so check the manifest file.
09:22 Ethan Park: Any notes on security/compliance for the Dedicated path? We need to know about encryption-in-flight and KMS.
09:29 Jordan Miller: For Dedicated, we support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated modes; hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default. We'll flag the SOC2/ISO docs in the follow-up.
09:38 Maya Rodriguez: Great. I'm comfortable with the plan.
09:41 Jordan Miller: Awesome. quick check — who owns the microburst run on your side?
09:45 Ethan Park: I'll own it.
09:47 Jordan Miller: Cool. Any other questions?
09:50 Sofia Li: No, thanks.
:09:52 Jordan Miller: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and schedule.
09:58 (call ends)
questions: Can we prefer predictability over average latency?; How to steer runtime to kernel choices?; Will prefix normalization reliably improve cache hit rate?; What are Dedicated burst cost estimates?
